issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, bus riding is not impossible but is hard to justify here because the rest of the profile provides no transport-related memory or appraisal content linking the trauma to buses or commuting. With Triggers strongly tied to Negative Appraisals in the formulation, the trigger set should plausibly connect to the appraisal themes; this item appears isolated.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: Self-blame can occur after trauma to a loved one, but in this profile it implies perceived causal responsibility for the loved one's trauma. That responsibility theme is not supported by the memory items, which are mainly sensory re-experiencing, nor by the other trigger content. The appraisal therefore feels insufficiently grounded in the rest of the selected profile.

For trauma to a loved one, 'Entrapment: Having no options' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which centers on victim-focused reminders and guilt about failing to protect others rather than a personal entrapment situation. It implies a different trauma context unless more detail is provided.

issues.item: Memory: Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
issues.explanation: 'Taste Vividness' is difficult to fit with the selected trauma type and the rest of the memory profile. In a loved-one trauma profile with auditory and narrative-fragmentation features, gustatory reliving is possible but here feels disconnected and unusually specific without any other sensory context supporting why taste would be central.

vignette: John, a 55-year-old Oceania man with a history of divorce and currently working as a nanny, first sought help after experiencing a profound sense of grief and emotional turmoil following an incident involving his young charge. The traumatic event occurred when John was caring for the child during a family gathering at the beach. He witnessed the tragic drowning of another child—a close friend of the child in his care—who struggled desperately while others tried to intervene, but tragically failed. Since that day, John has been haunted by vivid and intrusive memories of the incident. When he tries to recount the event, he often finds himself losing the thread of his narrative and unable to fully articulate what happened. The auditory recall is particularly distressing; when John remembers the moment, he hears the frantic cries for help, which replay incessantly in his mind. John’s experience of grief on recall is profound, and it intensifies with each memory. He feels overwhelmed by an overwhelming sense of loss and sorrow that leaves him feeling emotionally drained and vulnerable. The auditory memories are particularly potent triggers for these feelings, as they bring back the sounds of panic and despair from that fateful day. John’s negative appraisals have significantly impacted his ability to process and cope with these memories. He harbors a deep-seated belief that he is weak and inadequate because he failed to protect others during the incident. This sense of weakness has evolved into a feeling of dehumanization, where John often feels more like an object than a person capable of making a difference. The connection between his negative appraisals and memory is evident in how these beliefs exacerbate his grief on recall. Each time he attempts to recount the event, the belief that he failed to protect others intensifies his emotional distress. He has come to believe that if he were stronger or more competent, he could have prevented the tragedy, which leads him to feel even more helpless and dehumanized. John’s triggers, particularly visual reminders of body parts associated with the incident and conversations about people losing loved ones, are also significantly influenced by his negative appraisals. Whenever he sees something that reminds him of the drowning child or hears others discussing loss, John's belief in his own weakness resurfaces. This not only makes it difficult for him to engage with those around him but also heightens his distress when such triggers arise. In his current role as a nanny, these symptoms have taken a significant toll on John’s daily functioning and relationships. He has become increasingly withdrawn and avoidant of situations that might remind him of the event, including family gatherings or activities near water. This avoidance has strained his interactions with both the children he cares for and their parents, who are concerned about his emotional state. John's narrative is one of cyclical distress: each memory triggers his grief and sense of failure, which in turn intensifies his negative appraisals, making it even more difficult to cope with future memories or triggers. This cycle has left him feeling isolated and trapped by his own thoughts and fears. What finally brought John to seek help was the realization that he could no longer manage his daily responsibilities without becoming overwhelmed by these intense emotions and intrusive memories. He is most afraid of being unable to protect others again, but he also hopes for a sense of closure and healing—a way to reclaim his identity beyond this traumatic event.
